title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to evaluate whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. The archived execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Because the executed pipeline reused a single generated candidate per item for both conditions and no high‑confidence contamination flags occurred, the preregistered primary confirmatory estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) became degenerate and uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in web‑sourced corpora. Artifact‑verified outcomes: baseline = 150/150 passes, guarded = 150/150 passes; paired difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We (1) report these exact, archived numbers and the concrete artifact paths/hashes that substantiate them, (2) explicitly declare the preregistration→execution deviation that produced the degenerate test and cite the manifest evidence, (3) explain why specific detector persistence settings limit post‑hoc overlap inspection, and (4) provide artifact‑grounded, implementable recommendations (provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, and paraphrase‑robust detectors) to make future contamination audits sensitive to realistic leakage.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated repair. Operational decisions informed by benchmark results require that measured performance reflect model capability rather than dataset contamination (benchmark items appearing in model training data) or trivial templating. Meta‑analyses and recent surveys therefore call for contamination‑aware designs, deterministic fingerprinting, and verifier‑backed oracles.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered a confirmatory study (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to answer: under a conservative detector suite (exact equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds, provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those exclusions change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are threefold: (1) a fully preregistered, archived execution with deterministic reconciliation and validator traces; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150) with explicit citation to archived artifacts; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that documents why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes concrete, artifact‑anchored remedies for future audits.

Scope and bounded claims. Crucially, the executed run sampled deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and reused a single generated candidate per item for baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false). Both facts are recorded in the archived manifests cited below and they materially limit inference: the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM→NetOps and generate–validate pipelines. Recent system and benchmark work shows LLMs can produce concrete configuration artifacts from intent and propose repairs; integrating external verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality versus naive generation. Formal verification tools (e.g., Header Space Analysis and localized subspecification) are practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are widely used in generate–validate architectures.

Evaluation validity, contamination, and recommended defenses. Surveys and methodological critiques emphasize two recurring threats: (a) contamination—benchmark items or templates appearing in LLM training data can inflate apparent performance—and (b) construct invalidity—benchmarks dominated by templated or low‑complexity items may not reflect operational difficulty. Recommended defenses include deterministic fingerprinting (exact equality), fuzzy n‑gram overlap detectors, provenance timestamp checks, and reporting of detector score distributions. Our audit adopted a conservative subset of these defenses, focused on deterministic reproducibility and a validator‑backed binary outcome to limit ambiguity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The experiment was preregistered under study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 and froze detectors, the guarded exclusion policy, the sampling plan, and the analysis executor before any model outputs. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs, analyzed by paired_binary_analysis_v1 using exact McNemar two‑sided testing and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Planned sampling vs executed sampling (explicit preregistration→execution deviation). The preregistration listed four public benchmark sources (benchmark_scope entries: OpenAlex IDs corresponding to candidate public datasets). The executed run, however, sampled deterministic synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with source_identifier values that begin with "synthetic-netops:". This mismatch is a documented preregistration→execution deviation and is recorded in the archived per‑task manifest: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact path in the bundle; representative artifact hash: b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). The executed model configuration explicitly records independent_condition_generation = false (shared generation semantics) in execution/model_configuration.json (artifact hash: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). We therefore explicitly declare that the preregistered sampling_plan targeting public datasets was not followed: the execution used provenance‑stable synthetic sampling instead (archive evidence: execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json).

Generation semantics and their statistical effect. The preregistration allowed both independent per‑condition generation and a shared_initial_candidate mode; the archived execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), which performs a single model generation per item and reuses it for both baseline and guarded episodes unless a high‑confidence contamination exclusion triggers a replacement. This execution choice reduced model_calls_used to 150 (one shared call per item) instead of the preregistered potential of 300 independent calls; execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation are archived (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts) and confirm model_calls_used = 150.

Contamination detectors and persistence policy. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (and lower thresholds for sensitivity checks); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model training cutoffs. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred to limit archive size; this persistence policy is recorded in the pipeline transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json in the bundle). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred in this run, the detector did not persist a global per‑item overlap table; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty of flagged rows (artifact hash: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222) and a full overlap table is not present in the archive. We therefore report the artifact‑verified absence of high‑confidence flags and the absence of a persisted per‑item overlap distribution rather than invent per‑item overlap statistics.

Verifier and scoring rule. We used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the oracle (validator traces archived for every episode). The validator applies parsing→state update→property checks against the task payload (expected_final_state and workflow constraints) and yields a binary pass/fail under the preregistered scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation; per‑episode validator traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration) are archived in execution/scoring/*.json and formed the binary outcomes used in analysis.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The archived execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 300 and completed_episode_count = 300 (150 pairs), with model_calls_used = 150 (shared generation per item) and failed_episode_count = 0. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm completeness and consistent pair accounting (see deterministic_reconciliation artifact in the bundle; representative hashes cited above).

Contamination detectors: artifact‑verified absence of high‑confidence flags. The detector workflow produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows (artifact hash: 389227f0...). Because the detector persisted detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only on threshold crossings or replacements (transformation manifest policy), a global per‑item overlap table is not present in the archive for post‑hoc inspection.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics (exact archived numbers). The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table archived as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (artifact hash: c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e) is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode responses and validator traces are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl artifact hash: 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586) and substantiate these numbers.

Representative diagnostic. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) shows identical normalized_response and normalized_reference_answer and validator parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4 with score = VALID_CONFIGURATION. The per‑episode scoring JSON files in execution/scoring/ provide these traces and are included in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary confirmatory test became degenerate. Two artifact‑verified execution choices jointly produced the observed full concordance (n11 = 150): (A) the confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic items (execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with source_identifier beginning "synthetic-netops:"), and (B) the pipeline executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). Under these conditions, baseline and guarded episodes share the same generated candidate unless a high‑confidence contamination exclusion triggers a replacement; because no high‑confidence flags occurred, baseline and guarded outputs were identical by construction and the paired comparison cannot reveal generation‑level contamination or leakage into model training data for web‑sourced corpora. We therefore explicitly reclassify the preregistered primary confirmatory hypothesis as untestable/degenerate under the executed semantics and avoid any claim that the result generalizes to public benchmark contamination.

Detector persistence policy and interpretability consequences. The detector persisted per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred (per execution/transformation_manifest.json). This implementation choice reduced archive size but has a measurable interpretability cost: without a persisted per‑item overlap table we cannot report how close non‑flagged items were to the high‑confidence threshold (e.g., maximum overlap values). The archive therefore documents the absence of flagged events but not the distribution of gap distances to the threshold. To enable transparent sensitivity analysis, we recommend persisting per‑item overlap scores for every audit run (new artifact: analysis/contamination_scores.csv), a change that is implementable within the same pipeline and does not alter detectors or estimands.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations to increase audit sensitivity. Based on the recorded execution artifacts and the preregistered analysis plan, the following implementable changes will make future audits sensitive to realistic contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs/timestamps) rather than provenance‑stable synthetic items so provenance heuristics can detect pretraining‑era signals; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded generations are independent and discordant pairs are observable; (3) persist per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of threshold crossing to enable threshold‑sensitivity curves; (4) expand to multiple model instances (multi‑model replication) and independent seeds to increase expected discordance and power; (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline overlap cases. Each recommendation follows directly from explicit gaps visible in the archived outputs (model_calls_used = 150; empty analysis/contamination_summary.csv; absence of analysis/contamination_scores.csv) and can be implemented without inventing new detectors or validation logic.

Operational implications and limits of inference. The artifact‑verified pass rates confirm that the deterministic validator effectively enforces the preregistered functional constraints for the executed synthetic tasks. However, auditors should not extrapolate the executed null to public benchmarks: the archived record shows this run cannot detect paraphrase leakage, web‑sourced contamination, or multi‑model discrepancies. For operational NetOps risk assessment, audits should combine provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, cross‑model reconciliation, and human adjudication.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM→NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). This degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics; it therefore does not speak to contamination prevalence in independent public benchmarks. We explicitly document the preregistration→execution deviation (preregistered public benchmark sampling → executed deterministic synthetic sampling) and reclassify the primary confirmatory test as uninformative under the executed semantics. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, and paraphrase‑robust detectors—that the archived framework can adopt to produce informative contamination audits in future runs. All numbers and assertions above are supported by archived artifacts cited in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or private training corpora.

Executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") — absence of high‑confidence flags here does not imply absence of contamination in web‑crawled public benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and limiting sensitivity to generation‑level discordance.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact equality and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap); paraphrased memorization or subtler leakage may escape these heuristics without paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked properties for the executed tasks but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's modeled constraints.
